title: 08 — MLOps on Databricks End to End
html:
08 — MLOps on Databricks End to End

The one idea: a model in production is a versioned artefact with a known lineage, promoted by rules, served behind an endpoint that logs every request, and watched until the data moves away from what it learned. MLflow, Unity Catalog, Model Serving and Lakeflow Jobs each own one part of that loop.

1. What it is

---
title: The MLOps loop on Databricks
---
flowchart LR
    D["Features (UC tables,<br/>point-in-time)"] --> T["Train + track<br/>(MLflow runs, LoggedModel)"]
    T --> R["Register in Unity Catalog<br/>catalog.schema.model, versions"]
    R --> E["Evaluate challenger vs champion<br/>(overall and per segment)"]
    E -- "passes" --> A["Move @champion alias<br/>(approved)"]
    A --> S1["Batch scoring job<br/>(Lakeflow Jobs)"]
    A --> S2["Model Serving endpoint<br/>(real time)"]
    S2 --> L["Inference table<br/>(AI Gateway, UC Delta)"]
    S1 --> L
    L --> M["Monitor: drift, quality,<br/>delayed labels"]
    M -- "breach" --> T
Stage Databricks piece
Experiment tracking MLflow runs: parameters, metrics, artefacts. MLflow 3 LoggedModel ties a model to code, configuration, traces and evaluations
Registry Unity Catalog models: versions, aliases (such as @champion and @challenger), permissions, lineage to training tables
Batch inference A Lakeflow Job that loads models:/catalog.schema.model@champion and scores a table
Real-time inference Model Serving endpoint (custom model, foundation model or agent)
Request logging AI Gateway-enabled inference tables: requests and responses in a UC Delta table. Legacy inference tables could not be enabled on endpoints from 20 February 2026 (checked 2026-10-26)
Monitoring Data profiling and anomaly detection on inference and feature tables. Custom checks such as PSI
Retraining Jobs triggered on schedule, on table update, or on a monitoring breach. A model update trigger can start downstream jobs
CI/CD Declarative Automation Bundles (formerly Asset Bundles): jobs, endpoints and permissions as code

2. Why it matters

  • Without a registry and aliases, nobody can say which model produced last month's scores.
  • Without inference tables, you can't monitor, debug or retrain on real traffic.
  • Without promotion rules, a model that is better on average but worse for one segment reaches production.

3. The main ideas, beginner to expert

3.1 Beginner: track everything

Log the parameters, metrics, training data vintage (table version or snapshot), code commit, and the model with its input signature. Use mlflow.autolog() for supported libraries, and add your own tags for data vintage and owner.

3.2 Intermediate: aliases instead of stages

Unity Catalog models use aliases rather than the old workspace-registry stages (Staging and Production). Downstream code loads @champion, and promotion is just moving the alias, which is instant, auditable and reversible.

# Not run: requires Databricks with MLflow 3 and Unity Catalog.
import mlflow
mlflow.set_registry_uri("databricks-uc")
with mlflow.start_run() as run:
    mlflow.log_params(params)
    mlflow.log_metric("val_auc", val_auc)
    mlflow.set_tag("training_data_vintage", "fin.features.issuer_credit@v152")
    info = mlflow.sklearn.log_model(model, name="model", input_example=X_valid[:5],
                                    registered_model_name="fin.ml.downgrade_risk")

from mlflow import MlflowClient
MlflowClient().set_registered_model_alias("fin.ml.downgrade_risk", "challenger", info.registered_model_version)

# Batch scoring job: always load by alias.
score = mlflow.pyfunc.spark_udf(spark, "models:/fin.ml.downgrade_risk@champion")
spark.table("fin.features.issuer_today").withColumn("pd", score(*feature_cols)) \
     .write.mode("append").saveAsTable("fin.ml.downgrade_scores")

3.3 Senior: promotion rules, monitoring and governance

  • Promotion: the challenger must beat the champion overall and not regress on any important segment beyond a tolerance. A named person approves, as for a data release.
  • Shadow and canary: run the challenger on live traffic without acting on it, or send a small share of traffic to it, before full promotion.
  • Monitor three things:
    1. input drift (feature PSI),
    2. output drift (score distribution),
    3. performance once labels arrive (defaults are known months later, so plan for delayed labels).
  • Reproducibility: every score row records the model version, the input vintage and the methodology version.
  • Distributed training and tuning: Optuna for single-node tuning and Ray Tune for distributed tuning (Hyperopt is no longer maintained). For deep learning, use GPU compute or AI Runtime.

4. Working code

The script models a registry with aliases. It refuses a challenger that is better overall but worse for small issuers, then uses score PSI from an inference log to decide when to open a retraining ticket. numpy only.

import numpy as np

rng = np.random.default_rng(8)
# A registry in miniature: versions with metadata, and aliases that point at versions (like @champion).
registry = {"versions": {}, "aliases": {}}
def register(version, auc_by_segment, data_vintage, code_commit):
    registry["versions"][version] = {"auc": auc_by_segment, "data": data_vintage, "commit": code_commit}

register(3, {"all": 0.801, "small_issuers": 0.742, "large_issuers": 0.833}, "2026-06-30.v1", "a1b2c3d")
register(4, {"all": 0.812, "small_issuers": 0.701, "large_issuers": 0.851}, "2026-09-30.v1", "e4f5a6b")
registry["aliases"]["champion"] = 3
registry["aliases"]["challenger"] = 4

# Promotion rule: better overall AND no segment worse by more than 0.02 AUC. Averages hide harm to a segment.
def should_promote(champ, chall, tolerance=0.02):
    c, n = registry["versions"][champ]["auc"], registry["versions"][chall]["auc"]
    worse = [s for s in c if n[s] < c[s] - tolerance]
    return (n["all"] > c["all"] and not worse), worse
ok, worse = should_promote(registry["aliases"]["champion"], registry["aliases"]["challenger"])
print("promote v4:", ok, "| segments that got worse:", worse)

# Monitoring from an inference log: compare live score distribution with the training distribution.
train_scores = rng.beta(2, 8, 5000)
live_week = {"week 1": rng.beta(2, 8, 800), "week 6": rng.beta(3, 6, 800)}   # the population shifted
def psi(a, b, bins=10):
    edges = np.quantile(a, np.linspace(0, 1, bins + 1)[1:-1])
    pa = np.bincount(np.searchsorted(edges, a), minlength=bins) / len(a)
    pb = np.bincount(np.searchsorted(edges, b), minlength=bins) / len(b)
    pa, pb = np.clip(pa, 1e-4, None), np.clip(pb, 1e-4, None)
    return float(np.sum((pb - pa) * np.log(pb / pa)))
for week, scores in live_week.items():
    value = psi(train_scores, scores)
    action = "open retraining ticket" if value > 0.25 else "watch" if value > 0.1 else "none"
    print(f"{week}: score PSI {value:.3f} -> {action}")

Output:

promote v4: False | segments that got worse: ['small_issuers']
week 1: score PSI 0.008 -> none
week 6: score PSI 0.870 -> open retraining ticket

What to notice:

  • Version 4 has the better overall AUC (0.812 vs 0.801), but loses 0.041 on small issuers, so it is not promoted. An average-only rule would have shipped it.
  • Week 1 scores match training (PSI 0.008). By week 6 the population has shifted (PSI 0.870), which opens a retraining ticket before labels confirm the damage.

5. Common mistakes

  1. Loading models by version number in production code. Use aliases.
  2. No data vintage on runs. You can't reproduce or explain a model.
  3. Promoting on the average metric only.
  4. Waiting for labels to notice a problem. Monitor inputs and outputs from day one.
  5. Building on deprecated paths. Legacy inference tables and Hyperopt are being retired. Check status.

6. Exercise (2 hours, Databricks Free Edition)

  1. Train a small model in a notebook, log it with MLflow, and register it in Unity Catalog.
  2. Set @challenger and @champion aliases, and write a batch scoring job that loads @champion.
  3. Add a job task that computes score PSI against the training distribution, and fails if it exceeds 0.25.

7. Questions to test yourself

  1. Why load models by alias?
  2. What do AI Gateway-enabled inference tables record, and where?
  3. What three things should model monitoring cover?
  4. Why can a challenger with a better overall AUC still be rejected?
  5. What replaced Hyperopt on Databricks?

Answers

  1. Promotion and rollback become a single, audited alias move, with no code change.
  2. Requests and responses of serving endpoints, in a Unity Catalog Delta table.
  3. Input drift, output drift, and performance once labels arrive.
  4. It may be worse on an important segment. Averages hide that.
  5. Optuna for single-node tuning, and Ray Tune for distributed tuning.

8. Sources

Checked 2026-10-26 through web search.

  • AI Gateway inference tables: https://docs.databricks.com/aws/en/ai-gateway/inference-tables
  • Legacy inference tables: https://docs.databricks.com/aws/en/machine-learning/model-serving/inference-tables
  • Jobs triggers (including model update): https://docs.databricks.com/aws/en/jobs/triggers
  • Hyperopt deprecation note: https://docs.databricks.com/aws/en/machine-learning/automl-hyperparam-tuning/hyperopt-best-practices
